Note names in different languages

The same seven notes have different names around the world. English uses the letters C to B; Italy, France, Spain, Latin America, and many other countries sing Do Re Mi; Japan and Korea use both Do Re Mi and their own names. This chart lines them up, so you can read a score written for another country, or follow a teacher who uses another system.

The seven notes

Letters (English)CDEFGAB
Do Re Mi (fixed Do)DoReMiFaSolLaSi
Japanese ドレミ (katakana)ドレミファソラシ
Japanese ハニホハニホヘトイロ
Korean 도레미도레미파솔라시
Korean 다라마다라마바사가나
GermanCDEFGAH
Russian и др. (Cyrillic)ДоРеМиФаСольЛяСи
Chinese numbered (jianpu), in C major1234567
Indian sargam, in C majorSaReGaMaPaDhaNi

Each column is the same note (the white keys of a piano from C upward).

  • German calls B “H”, and uses “B” for B flat. A German score that says “B” means B♭.
  • Japanese ハニホ (ha-ni-ho) comes from the Japanese syllable order いろは. It is used mainly for key names: ハ長調 is C major, ト長調 is G major.
  • Korean 다라마 works the same way for key names: 다장조 is C major.
  • Sol is sometimes written “So”, and Si is “Ti” in the English-speaking tonic sol-fa tradition.
  • Chinese numbered notation (jianpu, 简谱) and the Indian sargam (Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni) count from the first note of the key, like movable Do; the row shows them in C major.

Sharps and flats

System♯ (F♯)♭ (B♭)
EnglishF sharpB flat
ItalianFa diesisSi bemolle
FrenchFa dièseSi bémol
SpanishFa sostenidoSi bemol
Japanese ドレミファ♯（ファのシャープ）シ♭（シのフラット）
Japanese ハニホ嬰ヘ (ei-he)変ロ (hen-ro)
Korean올림바 (ollim-ba)내림나 (naerim-na)
GermanFisB (not Hes)
RussianФа-диез (fa-diez)Си-бемоль (si-bemol)
Chinese numbered, in C major♯4♭7

How F sharp and B flat are said. German adds “-is” for a sharp and “-es” for a flat (Cis, Es, As), with B for B♭.

A sharp (♯) raises a note by a semitone, and a flat (♭) lowers it. In Note Namer the sign is written after the name: F♯, ファ♯, 파♯. For how the key signature changes the names, see sharps, flats, and key signatures.

Fixed Do and movable Do

Do Re Mi is used in two ways:

  • Fixed Do: Do is always C, whatever the key. This is how note names are used in Italy, France, Spain, and in many piano lessons in Japan.
  • Movable Do: Do is the first note of the key (in G major, G is Do). It shows how notes relate in the scale, and is common in singing classes and in Japanese and Korean school music.

Note Namer offers both. With a fixed system, C is always Do (ド, 도, До). With movable Do (and with the numbered and sargam names), the first note of the major key of the key signature is Do (1, Sa), so a minor key starts on La (6, Dha), the way it is taught in Kodály-style classes and in Japanese schools; notes outside the key get a sharp or flat. When the key signature changes in the middle of a piece, the names follow it.

Choosing the names in Note Namer

Above the score, Note names offers fixed names (ドレミ in katakana, C D E, Do Re Mi, 도레미, German C D E … H, and Cyrillic До Ре Ми) and names in the key (ドレミ or Do Re Mi with movable Do, Chinese numbered 1 2 3, and Indian Sa Re Ga). The first choice follows your browser's language, and the app remembers your choice. ハニホ and 다라마 are not offered. See the guide for the steps.
